name: Aretas
title: Nabatean king during Paul's time
summary: Aretas IV, with the nickname Philopatris ('the one who loves his people'), was ruler of the Nabatean kingdom based in the rock city of Petra. In the Bible, his name appears in Paul's second letter to the Corinthians, where the apostle tells how the king's governor (ethnarch) guarded the city of Damascus in order to arrest him. Paul escaped by being lowered in a basket through an opening in the city wall (2 Cor 11:32–33). This event sheds light on the political dangers faced by the first Christian preachers and on the Nabatean king's influence far beyond his own core territory. Before his conversion, Paul had stayed in 'Arabia' – likely Nabatean territory – which may have contributed to the hostility he later encountered. The Jewish historian Josephus reports that Aretas came into armed conflict with Herod Antipas after Herod divorced Aretas's daughter to marry Herodias, an event also reflected in the gospels' criticism of this marriage.

keyEvents.title: The governor's attempt to arrest Paul in Damascus
keyEvents.description: King Aretas' governor (ethnarch) kept watch over the city of Damascus with the aim of arresting the apostle Paul. Paul avoided capture by being lowered in a basket through an opening in the city wall. This event testifies to the political danger that early Christian preachers faced from various authorities.

keyEvents.title: Paul's stay in Arabia
keyEvents.description: After his conversion, Paul went to Arabia, an area under Nabatean rule. The Bible does not elaborate on what Paul did there, but several scholars have suggested that this stay may have aroused Nabatean opposition and contributed to the hostility he later experienced in Damascus under Aretas' governor.

keyEvents.title: The background of the conflict with Herod Antipas
keyEvents.description: Herod Antipas married Herodias after leaving his wife, who was the daughter of Aretas IV. The Gospels' mention of this marriage forms the biblical background for the military conflict between Aretas and Herodes described in detail by the Jewish historian Josephus. It should be noted that Aretas is not mentioned by name in the Gospels in this context.

footnotes.text: Aretas IV Philopatris ('the one who loves his people') ruled the Nabatean kingdom from about 9 BC to AD 40. The Nabataeans were an Arab people who controlled important trade routes between the Arabian Peninsula, Egypt, and the Mediterranean region, with Petra as their famous capital carved out of sandstone cliffs.

Archaeological finds in Petra, including inscriptions and coins minted with Aretas IV's name and portrait, confirm his reign and the kingdom's prosperity. The Nabataeans' sophisticated water systems, terraces, and monumental tomb facades testify to an advanced civilization.

The name 'Aretas' is the Greek form of the Nabatean name Ḥāritat (חָרִתַת). The Greek Ἁρέτας (Haretas) appears in 2 Cor 11:32. The name may mean 'the one who pleases' or 'the virtuous one' in Nabatean.

The Jewish historian Josephus (Antiquitates Judaicae 18.5.1–3) gives a detailed account of the conflict between Aretas IV and Herod Antipas. According to Josephus, Aretas defeated Herod militarily, and many Jews interpreted the defeat as God's punishment on Herod for the execution of John the Baptist.

Paul's mention of Aretas' ethnarch in Damascus (2 Cor 11:32) raises complex historical questions about Nabatean influence over the city. Some scholars argue that Aretas gained control of Damascus during a period when Roman dominance was weakened, while others believe the ethnarch led a Nabatean trade quarter within the city walls.

That Paul went to 'Arabia' (Gal 1:17) after his conversion likely means he traveled to the Nabatean kingdom. Several theologians have suggested that Paul may have carried out missionary work in this area, which potentially provoked Nabatean authorities and contributed to the hostility he later encountered in Damascus.

The Nabatean kingdom was eventually annexed by the Roman Empire in AD 106 under Emperor Trajan and became the Roman province of Arabia Petraea. However, during Aretas IV's time, the kingdom remained an important client state with significant autonomy and influence in the region.
